slides.title: Case study 3: reading a heart trace
slides.notes: Other problems of the same shape: a bearing fault from a vibration trace, a spoken digit from audio, a faulty weld from a current waveform.

runs.text: Case study 3: reading a heart trace
From a patient's ECG recording, decide between two classes: healthy, or myocardial infarction (a heart attack).
A raw ECG is thousands of samples per patient. Two healthy traces can look less alike than a healthy and a damaged one.
Cardiologists read it from subtle changes in shape and timing. There is no simple formula, but there are labelled examples.
Hagan, Neural Network Design, Chapter 25. The same design serves any "which class is this signal" problem.

slides.title: Feature extraction does half the work
slides.notes: In classical pattern recognition the features carry most of the engineering knowledge. The network only has to draw the boundary in feature space.

runs.text: Feature extraction does half the work
From a long signal to a few meaningful numbers
Feeding raw samples would need thousands of input weights and far more patients than exist.
Instead, measure what a cardiologist looks at: intervals, amplitudes and slopes.
Each feature means the same thing for every patient, whatever the recording length.
Fewer inputs, fewer weights, less data needed (L35).

slides.title: What the analysis found
slides.notes: This echoes the L38 fraud story: rare class, unequal costs, accuracy misleading.

runs.text: With many more patients in one class, a high accuracy can hide poor results on the smaller class. Read each row of the confusion matrix.
Calling a heart attack healthy is far worse than the reverse. The ROC curve lets the hospital choose a threshold that favours catching it.
Study the errors one by one
Misclassified records are often mislabelled, badly recorded, or a type of patient missing from the data. Each one is a lead.
Post-training analysis is not a final mark. It is how you find out what to fix in the data.

slides.title: Industry parallel: defect detection on a line
slides.notes: Ask the class for another example with rare positives and unequal costs: airport baggage screening, loan default, spam.

runs.text: Industry parallel: defect detection on a line
A camera photographs every circuit board, bottle or weld leaving a production line. A network decides: pass or reject.
Defects are rare, perhaps 1 part in 500. A missed defect reaches a customer; a false reject wastes a good part.
Extract features, train with cross-entropy, judge by confusion matrix, pick the threshold from the costs, and re-check when the product or lighting changes.
Swap "ECG" for "camera image" and "patient" for "part": the six steps do not change.

slides.title: Case study 4: mapping a forest with no labels
slides.notes: The measurements are cartographic: elevation, slope, aspect, distances to water, roads and past fire points, and hillshade at three times of day.

runs.text: Case study 4: mapping a forest with no labels
A national forest is divided into 30 m by 30 m cells. For each cell there are map measurements. Which cells are alike?
Nobody supplies the right answer. The network has to find the groups by itself. This is clustering.
It groups similar cells and also arranges the groups on a two-dimensional map, so ten measurements can be seen at once.
Hagan, Neural Network Design, Chapter 26: forest cover data from the US Forest Service.

slides.notes: Normalisation matters even more here than for an MLP: elevation in metres would swamp slope in degrees in every distance calculation. Take the map size and iteration count from the chapter.

slides.title: Reading the trained map
slides.notes: In the Hagan study the clusters can be compared afterwards with the known cover types, which were never shown to the network.

runs.text: Distance matrix of a trained map (illustrative). Dark: large distance between neighbouring neurons.
Three light regions, so three kinds of land
Dark ridges mark where the weights change sharply: the borders between clusters.
The hit histogram shows how much land falls in each region.
Weight planes say what defines a region: one may be high and steep, another low and near water.
Naming the clusters needs someone who knows forests. The network only finds them.

slides.title: Industry parallel: customer segmentation
slides.notes: Other uses of the same design: grouping sensor readings to find machine operating modes; grouping students by study pattern.

runs.text: A mobile operator has millions of prepaid customers. For each: recharge size and frequency, data used, calls made, time of day.
A handful of regions: heavy evening streamers, call-only users, weekend-only users. Marketing designs one plan for each.
Do the groups stay the same on next month's data? Does anyone in the business recognise them? If not, the clusters may be an accident.
Clustering has no test error. Stability and usefulness are the only proof.

slides.title: Your handwriting against a trained network
slides.notes: Expected findings: thin pen strokes, off-centre digits, a 7 with a crossbar, a 1 with a flag, lined paper. All differ from the training images.

runs.text: Your handwriting against a trained network
Open a digit recogniser trained on the MNIST data set. Hold printed digits to the webcam: nearly all are right.
Now volunteers write digits on paper with a ball pen and show them. Several are read wrongly.
Collect the failures on the board. What do they have in common?
The network scored 98% on its own test set. Why does it fail on digits written in this room?
Doodle Reader: teach it your shapes, then ask a classmate to draw.

slides.title: Domain shift: the data changed, the model did not
slides.notes: This is extrapolation (L40) in a pattern recognition setting. The inputs are outside the region the training data covered.

runs.text: Domain shift: the data changed, the model did not
Training and use did not match
Training digits: thick strokes, centred, size-normalised, white on black.
Classroom digits: thin pen, off-centre, on lined paper, local writing styles.
The test set came from the same source as the training set, so it could not warn us.
Close the gap between the two
Apply the same preprocessing at use as in training: centre, scale, thicken, invert.
Add examples collected where the model will be used.
Keep measuring after launch, and retrain when the error drifts.
